idiom_name: wrapper object holding an injected delegate + forwarding members over a shared interface
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the abstraction both sides share; give the wrapper a field holding the delegate, injected rather than constructed internally; implement each member of the abstraction by forwarding to the delegate, adding only the behaviour the wrapper exists for. Pass the receiver explicitly to the delegate only when the reuse must see the wrapper's overrides (true delegation), otherwise accept that self-calls inside the delegate stay with the delegate. Where the platform generates forwarding - a by-clause, struct embedding or a macro - declare the delegation and override only the members you change; hand-written forwarders are the fallback, not the goal. Keep the exposed surface as narrow as the clients need, and document ownership and receiver semantics explicitly.
code_sketch:
class Wrapper(Iface):                  # shares the interface with the delegate
    def __init__(self, delegate):      # the delegate is injected, not built in
        self.delegate = delegate
    def operation(self, arg):          # a forwarded member
        self.before()                  # only the wrapper's own behaviour
        return self.delegate.operation(arg)
# generated form, where the language has one:
#   class Wrapper(inner: Iface) : Iface by inner   # Kotlin writes the forwarders
pitfalls: Forwarding member-by-member by hand and letting the list drift when the interface changes.
Assuming the delegate sees the wrapper's overrides: self-calls inside the delegate stay inside the delegate.
Forwarding everything one-to-one with no added behaviour, which produces a middle man instead of reuse.
A method added to the delegate's interface but not forwarded by the wrapper surfaces only at call sites - no compile-time signal at the wrapper.
Sharing a mutable delegate between wrappers without synchronization: each wrapper observes the other's side-effects.
Storing a reference to a delegate that has been destroyed, producing a dangling or logically dead reference.

Python __getattr__ shadowing: explicitly defined instance attributes or properties on the wrapper take precedence over __getattr__ delegation, so inner-object attributes with the same name become unreachable unless using a pattern like Fast.ai's GetAttr.

Generated forwarding over-forwarding: Kotlin `by`, Go embedding and Ruby `Forwardable` forward every interface member automatically — if the wrapper does not intend to expose the full delegate interface, the generated forwarding exposes too much (violates interface segregation and creates a middle man).

Breaking the delegate's contract: a wrapper that forwards a subset of an interface (narrowing) may silently break callers that expect the full interface — the wrapper becomes only conditionally substitutable, which is invisible at compile time in statically typed languages.

Serialization and persistence gotchas: a wrapper that holds a delegate reference may serialize the delegate by reference or by value depending on serialization strategy, leading to deserialization surprises (stale references, duplicate objects, or deep-copy semantics that differ from the original).

Debugging opacity: when a delegated call fails, the stack trace points to the delegate's code, not the wrapper's call site — this can make it harder to trace why the wrapper invoked the delegate in the first place.

Memory leaks from circular references: if a delegate holds a reference back to the wrapper (intentionally or accidentally for callback purposes), and both are long-lived, the cycle prevents garbage collection unless one side uses a weak reference.

Wrong move: blanket-forwarding the whole surface via SimpleDelegator or method_missing so the wrapper's interface is invisible -> type checks, static analysis and stack traces no longer see the real surface and a renamed delegate method fails only at runtime -> instead declare the forwarded surface explicitly (Rails `delegate`, Kotlin `by`, an explicit forwarder list).

Wrong move: stacking `delegate` calls on an ActiveRecord model because one dot satisfies the Law of Demeter -> the model accumulates pass-throughs over grandchild tables and becomes refactor-proof glue -> instead delegate only from the aggregate root to its own children and move cross-entity behaviour into a service or form object.

Wrong move: a delegate protocol for a collaborator that always has exactly one implementation (the classic single-delegate Cocoa view) -> the indirection is ceremony with no polymorphism and every hook is a maintenance head-ache -> instead subclass the class or move the behaviour in unless genuinely swappable delegates exist.
